snippet.title: Great Scott! We’re Going Back to Our Technician Days
snippet.description:
What would you tell yourself if you could travel back to the day you earned your Technician-class amateur radio license? Would you buy different equipment, spend more time getting on the air, ask more questions—or avoid a few questionable radio purchases altogether?

In this episode of the Northeast Ham Radio Show, we are firing up the ham radio time machine and heading back to our Technician days. We’ll talk about the mistakes we made, the gear we probably did not need, the opportunities we missed, and the advice we wish someone had given us when we were brand-new operators.

Whether you just passed your Technician exam, are working toward your first ham radio license, or have been licensed long enough to remember your own beginner mistakes, join the conversation. What would you do differently—and what is the one piece of advice every new Technician needs to hear?

snippet.title: The Filter We Built for Ham Radio Is Now in Every Smartphone
snippet.description:
In 1880, Pierre and Jacques Curie discovered that certain crystals vibrate at precise frequencies when stressed with electricity. By the 1950s, amateur radio operators and engineers at Collins Radio in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, had turned that principle into razor-sharp mechanical and crystal filters, the components that finally made single-sideband voice communication practical on crowded shortwave bands.

Those filters did not stay in ham radio. The same piezoelectric technology evolved through surface acoustic wave and thin-film bulk acoustic resonator designs into something unrecognizable from the originals, and the stakes kept climbing. Today, a premium 5G smartphone carries close to one hundred of these filters, each one preventing its radios from drowning each other in interference. The companies manufacturing them control a $15.4 billion market.

This is the full lineage, from a Paris laboratory to your pocket.

snippet.title: Is KO4FX the Future of POTA & WWFF?
snippet.description:
In this episode of POTA PERformers, I sit down with Ethan, KO4FX / VA1VXD, a young amateur radio operator from Middle Tennessee who has built an impressive reputation in the portable ham radio world.

We talk about how Ethan got started in amateur radio through Skywarn, his first Parks On The Air activation at Stones River National Battlefield, and why POTA became such a big part of his ham radio journey. Living in an HOA with antenna restrictions and neighbourhood noise, Ethan found portable operating to be the perfect way to get on the air and make contacts from the field.

We also dive into operating style, fast-paced pileups, the classic “59” exchange, Canadian amateur radio licensing, Youth on the Air, Worldwide Flora and Fauna, Lakes on the Air, and even weak-signal 2-meter SSB.

If you are into POTA, WWFF, portable ham radio, youth in amateur radio, or chasing DX from the field, this is a conversation you will not want to miss.

📡 Topics covered:

Parks On The Air
Worldwide Flora and Fauna
Youth On The Air
Canadian amateur radio licensing
Portable ham radio operating
HOA antenna challenges
Fast-paced POTA activations
Lakes on the Air
2-meter SSB and weak-signal VHF

Thanks to Ethan, KO4FX, for joining me on POTA PERformers and sharing his story.

snippet.title: HF Propagation for Ham Radio Beginners

Have you ever wondered why 20 meters is open one day and completely dead the next? Why does 40 meters come alive after sunset? Why can you work Europe on 10 meters one afternoon, then hear almost nothing the following day?

Whether you're a newly licensed amateur radio operator or a seasoned ham looking to better understand the bands, this presentation explains the fundamentals that every HF operator should know.

Understanding propagation won't let you control the bands, but it will help you understand why they're behaving the way they are and make you a more effective HF operator.

snippet.title: Beginner’s Guide to Diodes
snippet.description:
Beginner’s Guide to Diodes

What does a diode actually do inside a radio or electronic circuit?

In this beginner-friendly reel, we explain the diode as a one-way valve for electricity and show why this small component is so important.

You will learn:

What anode and cathode mean

Why the stripe marks the cathode

The difference between forward bias and reverse bias

How diodes help turn AC into DC

How a protection diode can absorb damaging voltage spikes

How a diode can recover audio from an AM radio signal

The main difference between silicon, Schottky, Zener, LED, PIN and varactor diodes

Diodes appear throughout amateur radio equipment, including power supplies, receivers, transmitters, switching circuits, relay protection and signal detectors.

Once you understand the basic behaviour of a diode, many radio circuits become much easier to follow.

For amateur radio equipment, accessories and more beginner-friendly content, visit:

https://www.moonrakeronline.com
